questions.title: Nerve excitability is maximum at the firing level
questions.question: Regarding excitability of a nerve:

options.A: is maximum at the firing level.
options.C: can respond to a second stimulus during ARP.

explanations.A: Correct. Excitability changes across the course of an action potential: during the initial depolarization, as the membrane approaches the firing level (threshold), excitability rises and peaks right at that point, since the membrane is then closest to the self-sustaining Na+ influx that triggers a full spike. Through the rest of the action potential the fibre becomes refractory instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. During repolarization the fibre is within the absolute or relative refractory period, when excitability is reduced or abolished, not elevated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. No stimulus, however strong, can excite the fibre during the absolute refractory period (ARP) -- the Na+ channels needed for a second spike are simply unavailable until they recover.
explanations.D: Incorrect. During the relative refractory period (RRP) excitability is reduced, not zero -- a stronger-than-threshold stimulus can still trigger a second action potential, unlike during the ARP.

questions.learning_objective: State that nerve excitability is maximum at the firing level, and falls through the refractory periods that follow.

questions.title: Chronaxie is the time by double rheobasic strength to stimulate the nerve
questions.question: The Strength-Duration curve:

options.A: is the relationship between the duration of the stimulus and amplitude of response.
options.B: has a rheobase which is 2 times chronaxie.
options.C: has a chronaxie which is the time needed by double the rheobasic strength to stimulate the nerve.
options.D: strong stimuli of extreme short duration can excite the nerve.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The strength-duration curve relates a stimulus's intensity to the duration it must be applied to excite the nerve, not to the amplitude of the resulting response -- the action potential's amplitude is fixed by the all-or-none law, not a variable the curve tracks.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the two landmarks: chronaxie, not rheobase, is defined in terms of double an intensity -- specifically, double the rheobase intensity -- not the other way around.
explanations.C: Correct. Rheobase is the minimum stimulus intensity that can excite the nerve, however long it is applied. Chronaxie is the duration needed for a stimulus at exactly twice that rheobase intensity to excite the nerve, and it is used as an index of excitability -- a shorter chronaxie means a more excitable fibre.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Within limits a stronger stimulus needs a shorter duration to excite the nerve, but an extremely short-duration stimulus will not excite the nerve no matter how intense it is -- there is a floor duration below which no stimulus strength suffices.

questions.learning_objective: State that chronaxie is the duration needed for a stimulus at twice rheobase intensity to excite the nerve.

questions.title: Voltage-gated Na+ channel inactivation gates are open at rest
questions.question: Voltage-gated Na+ channels:

options.A: have activation gates on the inner surface of the membrane and inactivation gates on the outer surface.
options.B: inactivation gates are opened at rest.
options.D: at threshold potential, the inactivation gates close.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This reverses the two gates' actual positions: the activation gate sits near the outer surface and the inactivation gate on the inner surface, not the other way around.
explanations.B: Correct. At the resting membrane potential the voltage-gated Na+ channel's activation gate is closed and its inactivation gate is open, which together define the channel's resting state. Opening the outer (activation) gate on depolarization makes the channel activated; only later does the inner (inactivation) gate close, making it inactivated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Activation gates open on depolarization toward threshold, not specifically during catelectrotonus (the local hyperpolarization under a cathode-adjacent anode, or more generally an unrelated electrotonic phenomenon) -- the gate-opening event this question tests is tied to depolarization, not this specific named condition.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inactivation gates close shortly after the activation gates open, on a short delay following threshold, not exactly at the threshold potential itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that the voltage-gated Na+ channel's inactivation gate is open at rest, and its activation gate is closed.

questions.title: Chronaxie is a measurement of excitability
questions.question: Chronaxie is:

options.A: the time needed for the rheobase to stimulate a nerve fiber.
options.B: the minimum duration of a stimulus needed to excite the nerve.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The time needed for a stimulus at exactly rheobase intensity to excite the nerve is called the utilization time, not chronaxie -- chronaxie is instead defined at double the rheobase intensity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes utilization time (the duration at rheobase intensity), not chronaxie, which is defined at twice rheobase intensity, not the minimum intensity itself.
explanations.C: Correct. Chronaxie -- the duration needed for a stimulus at twice rheobase intensity to excite the nerve -- is used as an index of excitability: a shorter chronaxie indicates a more excitable fibre, and a longer one a less excitable fibre, which is exactly why clinicians and physiologists use it as a measurement of excitability. Because it is expressed as a simple duration, it is easier to compare across fibres or conditions than raw threshold-intensity values alone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "The utilization time" names a different landmark on the strength-duration curve -- the duration needed at rheobase intensity itself, not at double that intensity.

questions.learning_objective: State that chronaxie is used as a measurement (index) of nerve excitability.

questions.title: RMP in medium sized nerve is about -70 mV
questions.question: Resting membrane potential in medium sized nerve is normally about:

explanations.A: Incorrect. -50 mV is not the standard teaching figure for any of the cell classes whose RMP magnitude is typically taught -- large nerve/muscle fibres, medium neurons, or less excitable cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. +35 mV is not a resting value at all -- it is close to the overshoot value the membrane potential reaches at the peak of an action potential, not its resting state.
explanations.C: Incorrect. -90 mV is the standard teaching figure for large nerve fibres and large skeletal muscle fibres, a different (larger) class of cell than the medium-sized nerve fibre this question asks about.
explanations.D: Correct. RMP magnitude varies by cell type: about -90 mV in large nerve and skeletal muscle fibres, but about -70 mV in medium-sized neurons -- the class of fibre this question specifically names -- and only -20 to -40 mV in less excitable cells such as red blood cells and epithelium. Naming the wrong cell class for a given RMP value is one of the commonest slips on this fact.
explanations.E: Incorrect. -55 mV is not the standard teaching figure quoted for medium-sized nerve fibres; it falls between the taught values without corresponding to any of the three standard cell-type categories.

questions.learning_objective: State that the resting membrane potential of a medium-sized nerve fibre is about -70 mV, distinct from the -90 mV figure for large fibres.

questions.title: Myelinated fibre stimulation produces reversal of membrane potential
questions.question: The stimulation of myelinated nerve fibers would produce:

options.E: none of the above are correct.

explanations.A: Incorrect. An adequate stimulus produces an inward, not outward, flow of sodium ions -- Na+ moves down its electrochemical gradient into the cell, the mechanism of depolarization.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Potassium's movement during and after the action potential is outward (efflux), not inward, down its own concentration gradient.
explanations.C: Correct. An adequate stimulus to a myelinated fibre triggers a full action potential at the nearest node of Ranvier: depolarisation carries the potential from about -90 mV through the firing level to an overshoot of about +35 mV -- a genuine reversal of the membrane potential's sign, not merely a partial shift toward zero. This overshoot is the defining feature that separates a true action potential from a smaller, non-propagated local response.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stimulation of a myelinated fibre does not physically displace the myelin sheath; the sheath's job is passive insulation of the internode, unaffected in position by the electrical events of the action potential.
explanations.E: Incorrect, since option C correctly describes what stimulation of a myelinated fibre produces.

questions.learning_objective: State that stimulating a myelinated nerve fibre produces a reversal of the membrane potential (the overshoot), not merely partial depolarization.

questions.title: Local circuit conduction needs more energy than saltatory conduction
questions.question: Local circuit mechanism for conduction of action potential:

options.A: is more rapid than saltatory conduction.
options.B: occurs in the myelinated nerve fibers.
options.C: needs less energy than saltatory conduction.
options.D: needs more energy than saltatory conduction.
options.E: occurs in both myelinated and unmyelinated nerve fibers.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Local circuit (continuous, point-to-point) conduction is slower, not more rapid, than saltatory conduction -- saltatory conduction's node-to-node jumping is exactly what gives myelinated fibres their speed advantage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Local circuit conduction is the mechanism of unmyelinated, not myelinated, fibres; myelinated fibres instead use saltatory conduction between their nodes of Ranvier.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This has the comparison backwards: local circuit conduction needs more, not less, energy than saltatory conduction, for the same reason option D gives.
explanations.D: Correct. In an unmyelinated axon, the action potential must be freshly regenerated at every point along the membrane via local circuit current flowing to the next resting patch, so the whole membrane's Na+-K+ pump has to restore ionic gradients continuously along its entire length. Saltatory conduction, by contrast, regenerates the impulse only at the sparse nodes of Ranvier, which is far more economical -- so local circuit conduction needs more energy overall than saltatory conduction does.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Local circuit conduction occurs specifically in unmyelinated fibres; myelinated fibres instead conduct by the separate saltatory mechanism, so this option's claim of occurring in both is not correct.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that local circuit conduction in unmyelinated fibres needs more energy than saltatory conduction, since it regenerates the impulse continuously rather than only at the nodes.

questions.title: Relative refractory period coincides with second 2/3 of the descending limb
questions.question: Relative refractory period:

options.B: is a complete loss of excitability.
options.C: coincides with the second 2/3 of descending limb of spike.
options.D: during it the nerve can't respond to any stimulus whatever its strength.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The relative refractory period is a period of decreased, not increased, excitability -- only a stronger-than-threshold stimulus can excite the fibre during it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Complete loss of excitability describes the absolute, not the relative, refractory period; during the relative refractory period some Na+ channels have already recovered and are available.
explanations.C: Correct. The relative refractory period begins at the end of the absolute refractory period and ends when the membrane potential returns to its resting level -- a window that corresponds to roughly the second two-thirds of the spike's descending limb (repolarization), the first third of which is still part of the absolute refractory period. Only once enough Na+ channels have recovered, partway through repolarization, does the relative refractory period begin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This describes the absolute, not the relative, refractory period -- during the relative refractory period a sufficiently strong stimulus CAN still excite the fibre, unlike during the absolute refractory period.
explanations.E: Incorrect. After-hyperpolarization is a separate, later phase that follows repolarization, not the window the relative refractory period itself occupies.

questions.learning_objective: State that the relative refractory period coincides with the second two-thirds of the spike's descending limb.

questions.title: All-or-none law applies to a single nerve fiber
questions.question: All or none law can be applied to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A whole skeletal muscle is made of many individual fibres with different thresholds, so its overall contraction is graded (by recruiting more fibres and raising stimulation frequency), not all-or-none, even though each single fibre within it does obey the law.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A nerve trunk is a population of many individual fibres with different thresholds, so the compound action potential it produces is multi-peaked and graded, not fixed and all-or-none the way a single fibre's response is.
explanations.C: Correct. The nerve action potential obeys the all-or-none law at the level of a single nerve fibre: once triggered, it propagates with the same amplitude, duration and shape regardless of whether the stimulus was exactly at threshold or far above it, as long as conditions stay constant. A whole nerve trunk or muscle, by contrast, is a population of many such fibres with differing thresholds, so its overall response is graded rather than all-or-none.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Multi-unit smooth muscle is made of many independently-controlled fibres, each responding roughly individually to its own innervation, so the tissue's overall response is graded rather than all-or-none.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Single-unit smooth muscle fires as an electrically-coupled syncytium once a slow wave reaches its firing level, but the whole sheet's graded mechanical response (through varying wave frequency and coupling) is not the same fixed, all-or-none behaviour tested by this question at the single-fibre level.

questions.learning_objective: State that the all-or-none law applies to a single nerve fibre's action potential, not to a whole nerve trunk or whole muscle.

questions.title: Chronaxie: time by current of twice rheobase intensity
questions.question: The term "chronaxie "refers to:

options.B: the minimal duration of a stimulus which can excites the nerve.
options.C: the time needed by the rheobase to stimulate the nerve fiber.
options.D: the time needed by the current of twice the rheobase intensity to stimulate the nerve.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Utilization time is a related but different landmark -- the duration needed for a stimulus at exactly rheobase intensity, not at double that intensity, to excite the nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The minimal duration a stimulus of any strength could ever need corresponds more closely to the strength-duration curve's own asymptotic behaviour, not to chronaxie's specific double-rheobase definition.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The time needed by a stimulus at exactly rheobase intensity is utilization time, not chronaxie, which is instead defined at twice that intensity.
explanations.D: Correct. Chronaxie is the duration needed for a stimulus at twice rheobase intensity to excite the nerve -- a specific, standardised point on the strength-duration curve used as an index of excitability. A shorter chronaxie therefore signals a more excitable fibre, and a longer one a less excitable fibre.
explanations.E: Incorrect, since option D correctly defines chronaxie.

questions.learning_objective: Define chronaxie as the duration needed by a stimulus at twice rheobase intensity to excite the nerve.

questions.title: Chronaxie is inversely proportional to excitability
questions.question: Chronaxie is:

options.A: the duration of the rheobase stimulus.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The duration of a rheobase-intensity stimulus is utilization time, a different landmark from chronaxie, which is defined at twice, not exactly at, rheobase intensity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Double rheobase stimulus" names an intensity, but chronaxie is itself a duration -- specifically, the duration needed by a stimulus at that doubled intensity to excite the nerve, not the intensity value itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Utilization time is the duration at rheobase intensity, a related but distinct landmark from chronaxie's double-rheobase definition.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chronaxie is not the rheobase stimulus itself; rheobase is an intensity (the threshold current), while chronaxie is a duration measured at twice that intensity.
explanations.E: Correct. Chronaxie is used as an index of excitability, and the relationship runs inversely: a more excitable fibre needs only a very brief duration at twice rheobase intensity to fire, giving it a short chronaxie, while a less excitable fibre needs a longer duration, giving it a long chronaxie. This inverse relationship is exactly why chronaxie is used clinically as a quick index of a nerve's excitability.

questions.learning_objective: State that chronaxie is inversely proportional to excitability -- a shorter chronaxie means a more excitable fibre.

questions.title: Deep pressure decreases conduction mainly in A-type fibres
questions.question: Which of the following is correct for nerve fibers:

options.B: B fibers are faster than A fibers.
options.C: postganglionic nerve fibers are of B type.
options.D: preganglionic nerve fibers are of C type.
options.E: deep pressure decreases conduction mainly in A type.

explanations.A: Incorrect. C fibres are unmyelinated, not myelinated -- they are the thinnest, slowest-conducting class of the three (A, B, C).
explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the actual speed ranking: A fibres (2-20 micrometres, 20-120 m/sec) conduct faster than B fibres (1-5 micrometres, 5-15 m/sec), not the other way around.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Postganglionic autonomic fibres are the example given for C fibres, not B fibres.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Preganglionic autonomic fibres are the example given for B fibres, not C fibres.
explanations.E: Correct. Beyond conduction speed, the fibre classes differ in their sensitivity to environmental factors: local anaesthetics depress transmission in C fibres before A fibres, B fibres are the most susceptible to hypoxia, and deep pressure on a nerve can abolish conduction in A fibres while C fibres stay relatively intact -- so deep pressure decreases conduction mainly in A-type fibres. This differential vulnerability is a classic bedside correlate: a limb "falling asleep" under sustained pressure loses touch and motor (A-fibre) sensation before it loses dull, aching pain (C-fibre) sensation.

questions.learning_objective: State that deep pressure on a nerve decreases conduction mainly in A-type fibres, one of several differential sensitivities distinguishing the A, B and C fibre classes.
